title: Half-life and uses of radiation
examTip: Half-life calculations: each half-life halves the activity. After n half-lives, remaining activity = initial × (1/2)ⁿ. Read this off a graph, or calculate it. The exam often gives you a decay graph. It asks you to find the half-life. See how long the activity takes to drop from one value to exactly half.
introTips: Radioactive decay is random. You cannot predict when any one nucleus will decay. But with large numbers, the overall rate is very predictable.
Half-life is the time for half the undecayed nuclei to decay. In other words, it is the time for the count rate (or activity) to halve.
A short half-life means the substance decays quickly. This is useful for medical tracers. A long half-life means it stays radioactive for a very long time.
Contamination means unwanted radioactive material gets onto or into something, such as your body. Irradiation means being exposed to radiation. These are different hazards.
Uses of radiation match the type of radiation to the job. Gamma is used to explore internal organs and to treat cancer.
intro: Every radioactive substance decays at its own rate. Some radioactive isotopes are so unstable that they decay in milliseconds. Others decay so slowly that they will carry on for billions of years. Half-life is how we measure this rate. It turns out to be one of the most useful ideas in all of science. It helps doctors give targeted cancer treatments. Half-life also tells you how long radioactive waste stays dangerous. That is central to debates about nuclear power.

keyPoints.heading: What half-life means
keyPoints.content: Half-life is the time it takes for the number of nuclei of a radioactive isotope in a sample to halve. It is also the time for the count rate (or activity) from the sample to fall to half. Radioactive decay is random. You cannot predict which nucleus will decay next, or when. But with very large numbers of atoms, the overall rate is predictable. This is why half-life is a reliable measure, even though each decay is random. Activity (measured in becquerels, Bq) is the number of decays per second. The count rate is the number of decays a detector records each second. - After 1 half-life: activity = A₀/2 - After 2 half-lives: activity = A₀/4 - After 3 half-lives: activity = A₀/8 - After n half-lives: activity = A₀ × (½)ⁿ The number of undecayed nuclei halves at the same rate as the activity. You can also give the fall as a ratio. After 2 half-lives, the activity is 1/4 of its starting value. So the net decline is 3/4 of the starting activity.
writeBullets: Half-life — the time for the undecayed nuclei to halve, or for the count rate (or activity) to fall to half
Activity is measured in becquerels (Bq) = number of decays per second
Radioactive decay is random. You cannot predict single decays, but the overall rate is predictable
After n half-lives: activity = initial activity × (½)ⁿ
After 2 half-lives, 1/4 of the activity is left: a net decline of 3/4
Decay graph: a curved line that falls steeply, then flattens. It never reaches zero

The number of radioactive decays per second; measured in becquerels (Bq)
The unit of radioactive activity; 1 Bq = 1 decay per second
The number of decays recorded each second by a detector

keyPoints.memTip: Each half-life, divide the activity by 2. After 3 half-lives, divide by 8 (= 2 × 2 × 2).
keyPoints.tutor_note: Practise reading half-life from a graph. Find a point, then find half that value. Read the time difference from the x-axis.

keyPoints.heading: Reading and drawing decay graphs
keyPoints.content: A radioactive decay graph shows activity (Bq) or count rate on the y-axis and time on the x-axis. The shape is always a curved decrease that approaches but never reaches zero. This is an exponential decay curve. To find the half-life from a graph: (1) pick any starting activity value (for example, 800 Bq) (2) find half that value (400 Bq) (3) read the time at 800 Bq (t₁) and the time at 400 Bq (t₂) (4) half-life = t₂ − t₁ You can check by repeating from 400 Bq → 200 Bq. The time interval should be the same. To draw a decay graph, plot points at each half-life (0, t½, 2t½, 3t½, ...). The activity halves each time. Then join them with a smooth curve. The curve must never touch or cross the x-axis.
writeBullets: Decay graph: an exponential curve. Steep at first, flattening slowly, never reaching zero
To find half-life: pick an activity value, find half of it, and read the time difference
Half-life is constant. It takes the same time to go from 800→400 Bq as from 400→200 Bq
To draw: halve the activity at each half-life. Join with a smooth curve that never touches the x-axis
Activity (Bq) or count rate on the y-axis. Time (s, min, hours or years) on the x-axis

keyTerms.def: A curve where the quantity halves in equal time intervals — the shape of all radioactive decay graphs
A graph of activity vs time showing an exponential curve — used to determine half-life

keyPoints.memTip: Pick any two points where the activity halves. The time between them is the half-life. Check it is the same anywhere on the curve.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Practise both reading half-life from graphs AND drawing decay curves. Both come up in exams.

keyPoints.heading: Uses of nuclear radiation
keyPoints.content: Different radioactive isotopes are chosen for different jobs. The choice depends on their type of radiation and their half-life. In medicine, nuclear radiation is used in two ways. Exploring internal organs: a radioactive isotope, called a tracer, is injected or swallowed. It travels to the organ and is detected by a camera outside the body. It must give out gamma rays, so the radiation gets out through the body. It must have a short half-life, so the patient's dose stays low. Controlling or destroying unwanted tissue: this is called radiotherapy. A focused beam of gamma rays can be aimed at a tumour (a lump of cancer cells). Or a radioactive source can be placed inside the body, close to the tumour. The radiation kills the cancer cells. Weighing up the risks: both uses expose the patient to ionising radiation, which can damage healthy cells. Doctors use them when the benefit is greater than the risk. A scan may find an illness early. Radiotherapy may cure a cancer. People often feel radiation is more dangerous than the data show. When you evaluate a use, compare the data on risk with what happens with and without it.
writeBullets: Medical uses: exploring internal organs, and controlling or destroying unwanted tissue
Tracer — gamma emitter with a short half-life. Injected or swallowed, then detected outside the body
Radiotherapy — radiation kills the cancer cells in a tumour. It can come from a gamma beam or a source inside the body
To evaluate a use, weigh the benefit against the risk, using the data given

keyTerms.def: A radioactive isotope (gamma emitter, short half-life) used to explore internal organs; detected outside the body
Using a focused beam of radiation to control or destroy unwanted tissue, such as a tumour

keyPoints.memTip: Tracer: gamma + short half-life. Radiotherapy: radiation aimed at the tumour.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Exams often ask 'why must the tracer have a short half-life?'. Answer: to keep the patient's total radiation dose as low as possible.

keyPoints.heading: Contamination, irradiation and radiation dangers
keyPoints.content: Irradiation: exposing an object to nuclear radiation. The irradiated object does not become radioactive. If the source is outside, removing or shielding it stops the irradiation. Example: standing near a radioactive rock. Contamination: the unwanted presence of materials containing radioactive atoms on other materials. On a person, it may be on skin or clothes, or swallowed or breathed in. The hazard comes from the decay of the contaminating atoms. A contaminated object carries the radioactive material with it. They keep irradiating you, even when you move away from other sources. It is much harder to deal with. The type of radiation affects the hazard. It is very dangerous if it is an alpha emitter. Alpha is highly ionising inside the body. Why radiation is dangerous: - ionising radiation knocks electrons off atoms in body cells - this damages DNA, causing mutations - mutations can cause cancer (uncontrolled cell division) - mutations in reproductive cells can be passed on to children The risk grows with the dose and depends on the type of radiation. Alpha is the most ionising, so it is the most dangerous inside the body. Half-life and hazard: radioactive isotopes have a very wide range of half-lives. For the same number of nuclei, a short half-life means a high activity at first. It is very dangerous, but only for a short time. A long half-life means a lower activity. But it stays a hazard for a very long time. Protection: distance, shielding (lead or concrete) and keeping exposure time short. Sharing results: studies of how radiation affects people are published and shared with other scientists. Then other scientists can check the findings. This is called peer review.
writeBullets: Irradiation — exposing an object to nuclear radiation. The object does not become radioactive. An outside source can be removed or shielded
Contamination — unwanted radioactive atoms on or in other materials. The hazard comes from their decay
Ionising radiation damages DNA → mutations, which can cause cancer
Alpha is the most dangerous in contamination. It is highly ionising near body cells
Short half-life: high activity, but not for long. Long half-life: lower activity, but a hazard for a long time
Protection: increase distance, use lead or concrete shielding, keep exposure time short
Studies of radiation effects are published so other scientists can check them (peer review)

The unwanted presence of materials containing radioactive atoms on other materials; the hazard comes from their decay

0.question: A radioactive sample has an initial activity of 640 Bq. After 3 half-lives, what is the activity?
0.correctFeedback: Correct! After 3 half-lives: 640 → 320 → 160 → 80 Bq. Each half-life divides by 2. So after 3: 640 ÷ 8 = 80 Bq.
0.wrongFeedback: Divide by 2 three times: 640 → 320 → 160 → 80 Bq. Or use: 640 × (½)³ = 640 × (1/8) = 80 Bq.

1.question: On a decay graph, the activity falls from 600 Bq to 300 Bq in 4 hours. How long does it take to fall from 300 Bq to 150 Bq?
1.correctFeedback: Correct! Each fall to half takes one half-life. The half-life is 4 hours, so 300 Bq to 150 Bq also takes 4 hours.
1.wrongFeedback: The half-life stays the same. Going from 600 Bq to 300 Bq is one half-life, 4 hours. So 300 Bq to 150 Bq also takes 4 hours.

2.question: Why must the radioactive tracer used in medical imaging have a short half-life?
options: To keep the patient's total radiation dose as low as possible
To make it easier to detect outside the body
So the tracer reaches all organs equally
To stop the tracer decaying before it is injected
2.correctFeedback: Correct! With a short half-life, the tracer quickly decays to a very low activity. So the patient gets a much smaller total radiation dose.
2.wrongFeedback: The half-life must be short to keep the total radiation dose low. Once the imaging is done, you want the activity to fall quickly. Then the patient is not exposed to ongoing radiation.

3.question: What is the key difference between contamination and irradiation?
options: Contamination: radioactive material is on or in the body, and keeps irradiating you as you move. Irradiation: exposure from an outside source, which stops when the source is removed
Contamination is always from gamma radiation. Irradiation is always from alpha
Contamination only affects the skin. Irradiation affects internal organs
Irradiation means the body becomes radioactive. Contamination does not
3.correctFeedback: Exactly right! Contamination: radioactive material is on or in the body, so the risk goes wherever you go. Irradiation: an outside source. Remove or shield the source, and the exposure stops.
3.wrongFeedback: The key difference is location. Contamination = radioactive material on or in the body (it stays with you). Irradiation = an outside source (it stops when the source is removed or shielded).

commonMistakes: Dividing by n instead of using (½)ⁿ. After 3 half-lives, divide by 8 (= 2³), not by 3.
Saying the activity falls to zero after a few half-lives. It only halves each half-life, so it keeps getting smaller. The smooth curve on a decay graph never touches zero.
Mixing up contamination and irradiation. Contamination means radioactive material is on or in the body. Irradiation is outside exposure only.
Choosing an isotope with the wrong half-life for a medical tracer. A very long half-life gives a needlessly high radiation dose. Too short, and it decays before the imaging is done.
Forgetting to explain why a medical tracer must give out gamma. It must pass through the body to reach a camera outside. Alpha or beta would be absorbed before reaching the detector.
examTips: To find half-life from a graph: pick a clear starting point and halve the activity. Read both times from the x-axis and subtract. Check your answer by repeating from the second point.
After n half-lives: remaining activity = initial × (½)ⁿ. If you are not confident with powers, build a step-by-step table.
For 'why gamma for a medical tracer' questions: (1) gamma passes through tissue. So it can be detected outside the body. (2) A short half-life means the dose falls quickly after the scan.
Contamination is harder to deal with than irradiation, because the source stays with you. Mention this when explaining why alpha contamination is so dangerous.
In evaluation questions, use the data given. Weigh the benefit of the use against the risk from the radiation.
